excerpt: How a parent or guardian files an injury claim for a child in Georgia or South Carolina, and how the deadline differs from an adult's.
keyTakeaways: Parents and legal guardians can file personal injury claims on behalf of injured children in both Georgia and South Carolina. Georgia's statute of limitations for minors is tolled until age 18 under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90, giving children until their 20th birthday to file (medical malpractice claims run on a shorter clock, O.C.G.A. § 9-3-73). South Carolina's tolling provision (S.C. Code § 15-3-40) extends the deadline only to one year past the child's 18th birthday — age 19 — or three years from the injury if that is later. Both states require court approval for larger minor settlements — above $25,000 in Georgia and above $2,500 in South Carolina — with the money paid to a conservator, into a court-restricted account or into a structured settlement. Recoverable damages include medical costs, future earning capacity, pain and suffering, and emotional impact.

faqs.question: Who can file a personal injury claim on behalf of an injured child?
faqs.answer: In both Georgia and South Carolina a parent, a court-appointed guardian or conservator, or another adult acting as the child's next friend can file the claim — O.C.G.A. § 9-11-17(c) in Georgia and Rule 17(c) of the South Carolina Rules of Civil Procedure. Non-custodial parents may also have standing, though custodial parents typically take the lead in filing.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a child's injury claim in Georgia?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, the standard personal injury statute of limitations is 2 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). However, for minors, the clock is tolled (paused) under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90 until the child turns 18. This means the child has until their 20th birthday to file. Medical malpractice claims, including birth injuries, run on a shorter clock under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-73. Parents may still file during the child's minority, and doing so promptly is generally advisable to preserve evidence.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a child's injury claim in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina's personal injury statute of limitations is 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). For minors, S.C. Code § 15-3-40 pauses the clock during childhood but caps the extension at one year after the child turns 18 — so the deadline is the child's 19th birthday, or three years from the injury if that comes later. Medical malpractice claims are capped separately under S.C. Code § 15-3-545. As with Georgia, filing promptly is recommended because witness memories fade and evidence deteriorates over time.

faqs.question: Do minor injury settlements require court approval?
faqs.answer: Yes, above modest amounts. In Georgia any settlement worth more than $25,000 must be approved by the probate court, or by the court hearing the case once suit is filed (O.C.G.A. § 29-3-3). In South Carolina a settlement worth more than $2,500 after fees needs court approval — the circuit or probate court up to $25,000, and the circuit court alone above that (S.C. Code § 62-5-433). The court reviews the settlement to ensure it is in the child's best interest, and the funds are paid to a conservator, into a court-restricted account or into a structured settlement until the child reaches 18.

faqs.question: What types of damages can an injured child recover?
faqs.answer: An injured child can recover medical expenses (current and future), pain and suffering, lost future earning capacity, emotional and developmental impact damages, and costs of ongoing rehabilitation or therapy. Parents may separately recover the medical bills they paid and the value of the child's lost services. The calculation of future damages often requires expert testimony from medical and economic specialists.
